_what_this_is: P526: the charter is soft, negotiated and contributed to by the factory. 'The answer lies in the architectural commitment to the hard cast of the kernel, which is ultimately a kind of live-or-die button whose threat is continuously invoked -- "Here is a new charter; if it cannot be satisfied beyond what is priced as acceptable, then the factory needs to be scrapped."'
_why_a_separate_file: The separation has to be architectural or it is decorative. charter.json is writable by the factory at its metrics layer; this file is not writable by the factory at all. That is the same split the exoharness spec draws between a trusted substrate and the semantics above it, and for the same stated reason: keeping the committed part minimal 'maximizes the space of behaviors that can evolve above it'. Note the asymmetry that makes this the harder half -- exo's own footnote records that its equivalent is a POLICY, technically permissive, disallowed by default configuration. Ours is a stipulation too. Neither is a wall. Saying so is the point.
_what_this_is_not: It is not a safety limiter. max_live_voices and the master limiter live in policy.json and exist so a wrong parameter cannot destroy the speakers. Those protect the equipment. This protects the identity: it is the set of conditions under which this is no longer the factory the architect committed to, and should be scrapped rather than repaired.

identity.k1_concatenative: The factory assembles from recorded grains. It does not synthesise from scratch. A version that stops being concatenative is a different factory.
identity.k2_continuous: The factory runs forward without beginning or end. 'A factory with a start and an end is a work; a factory that only runs forward is a factory.' A version that renders fixed-length pieces is a different factory.
identity.k3_behaviour_outside_code: Behaviour lives in data the factory re-reads while running. A version that requires recompilation to change what it does has lost the r > 0 property (P75) that the whole enterprise rests on.

scrapping_conditions._when_the_button_is_pressed: Three or more charter metrics failing, or any never_tolerated metric failing, sustained across two consecutive runs of at least 100 windows.
scrapping_conditions._two_runs_not_one: One bad run is a run. The 24 Aug ablation lost two runs to a squatted UDP port and one to a starved buffer load, none of which was the factory's doing. A single-run trigger would have scrapped a healthy factory three times in one day.
scrapping_conditions._and_what_scrapping_means: Not deletion. It means this charter edition is declared unsatisfiable BY THIS FACTORY, and either the charter is re-priced (new edition, recorded as such) or the factory is rebuilt. Both are governance acts and both are logged. What must not happen is quietly widening a bound until the run passes -- which is the failure that would make this entire file theatre.

_enforcement:
ARMED at edition 2, 1 Sept 2026. Edition 1 deferred enforcement until 'the charter has been evaluated against enough runs to know whether its bounds are honest'. That condition is now met and the evidence is recorded here so a later reader can judge it rather than trust it.

CHARTER HONESTY, across ten runs of >= 100 windows (tools/charter_honesty.py): seven of eight metrics discriminate, i.e. each both passes and fails somewhere. m1, m3, m4, m5, m7 have departed; m2_level and m8_in_band came within 2% and 1% of a bound without crossing. ONE metric is decorative: m6_texture is bounded [2,5] while policy.json pins voices to [2,4], so it restates a setting and can never carry information about the factory. It should be replaced, and moving its bound would be the wrong repair.

THE GUARD IS TESTED, NOT ASSUMED (tools/test_kernel_guard.py). It fires on both historical master_gain pairs of 31 Aug and stays silent on both healthy pairs of 28 and 30 Aug. This project has shipped three guards that reported diligently and could not act -- a .try around capture rotation, an alignment check whose exit status was piped into tail, and an archive verify that compared stale audio against its own stale checksums -- so a guard that has never fired is not yet distinguishable from one that cannot.

FIRING ON AN ARCHITECT'S ERROR IS INTENDED BEHAVIOUR. Edition 1 deferred enforcement to avoid 'killing the factory for the architect's arithmetic errors'. Both would-be firings in the recorded history were exactly that, a mis-set master_gain, and both were correct: m3 read 0.205 against a bound of 0.02, and this charter calls clipping 'not an aesthetic departure, it is a broken transport'. The factory should have stopped. Every measurement taken at the stream output missed it because the limiter hid it downstream. A kernel that fires only on the factory's own errors would assume the party that moves first cannot be wrong (P285), which is a strange thing for a Stackelberg leader to assume about himself.

DRY RUN RECORD: 18 journalled decisions, 0 would-fire, all correctly declining because sustained failures stayed within tolerance.
_what_arming_does: kernel_guard.py --arm stops the factory when the scrapping condition holds across two consecutive runs of >= 100 windows. It stops; it does not delete, does not edit the charter, and cannot widen a bound. P458: nothing here may be unrecoverable, and a stopped factory restarts with one command. Restarting is a governance act and is journalled to kernel_journal.jsonl.
